**Key Points:**


- The right home loan depends on factors such as your budget, down payment, credit, eligibility and plans for the home
- Home loan options differ in how rates work, qualification requirements, upfront costs and ongoing expenses
- A 20% down payment isn’t required for many home loans, and some buyers may also qualify for down payment assistance
- Current homeowners have borrowing options too, including home equity loans and cash-out refinancing


A new home may be on your horizon, or you may be thinking about what’s possible with the one you already own. Either way, your home, goals and financial situation are one-of-a-kind. Your financing should reflect that.


The loan you choose can affect your upfront costs, monthly payment and finances for years to come. Let’s look at the most common home loan options and the questions that can help you narrow your choices.


## What Are the Main Types of Home Loans?


The main home loan options include conventional, FHA and VA loans, along with adjustable-rate and jumbo mortgages. Current homeowners may also consider home equity loans or a cash-out refinance to borrow against the equity they’ve built.


These categories can overlap, because some are defined by who backs the loan and others by how the interest rate works or how much you need to borrow. A jumbo loan, for example, may have a fixed or adjustable rate. A cash-out refinance isn’t a separate category either. It’s available with conventional, FHA, VA and jumbo loans.


Here’s a closer look at how each option works:


### Conventional Fixed-Rate Loans


A[conventional fixed-rate mortgage](https://www.pennymac.com/conventional-home-loans) is a mortgage that isn’t insured or guaranteed by a government agency. With a fixed-rate loan, your interest rate, monthly principal and interest payment stay the same for the entire loan term. A conventional fixed-rate loan may let you:


- Buy a home with as little as 3% down
- Avoid mortgage insurance with a 20% down payment
- Keep the same interest rate for the life of the loan
- Choose from fixed-rate loan terms ranging from 10 to 30 years with Pennymac
- Use for a home purchase or to refinance an existing mortgage


### FHA Loans


A[Federal Housing Administration (FHA) loan](https://www.pennymac.com/fha-home-loans) is a government-backed mortgage with flexible credit score requirements and low-down-payment options. It can be a favorable option for first-time homebuyers or those with less established credit. An FHA loan may let you:


- Buy a home with as little as 3.5% down
- Qualify with more flexible credit and debt-to-income guidelines than conventional loans typically allow
- Refinance an existing FHA loan with an FHA Streamline Refinance, if eligible


### VA Loans


[VA loans](https://www.pennymac.com/va-home-loans) , guaranteed by the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs, are available to eligible veterans, active-duty service members and certain surviving spouses. They can be used to purchase a primary residence or refinance an existing mortgage.


For qualified borrowers, VA loans may offer:


- A $0 down payment option for a home purchase, subject to eligibility and property requirements
- No monthly mortgage insurance
- Flexible qualification guidelines
- [VA Streamline Refinance (IRRRL)](https://www.pennymac.com/refinancing-products/va-irrrl-streamline-refinance) and cash-out refinance options for eligible homeowners


### Adjustable-Rate Mortgages (ARMs)


An[adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM)](https://www.pennymac.com/adjustable-rate-mortgages-arms) begins with a fixed interest rate for a set introductory period. After that, the interest rate can periodically change based on market conditions and the terms of the loan.


ARMs may offer:


- A lower initial rate than a comparable fixed-rate mortgage
- Lower initial monthly principal and interest payments
- A fixed introductory period that may align with plans to move, sell or refinance within a few years


After the introductory period, your rate and monthly principal and interest payment may rise or fall based on the loan’s terms and market conditions.


### Jumbo Loans


A[jumbo loan](https://www.pennymac.com/blog/homebuyers-guide-to-jumbo-loans) can be used to buy or refinance higher-priced homes that require a larger loan amount. Jumbo loans apply when the amount borrowed exceeds the conforming loan limit, which is the maximum loan amount set each year by the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) for most conventional mortgages.


For 2026, the baseline[conforming loan limit for a one-unit property is $832,750](https://www.fhfa.gov/news/news-release/fhfa-announces-conforming-loan-limit-values-for-2026) , with higher limits in designated high-cost areas.


Some jumbo loan basics:


- Finance up to $3.5 million
- Eliminate the need for secondary financing
- No prepayment penalty with Pennymac
- Typically best suited to borrowers with strong credit and healthy reserves


### Home Equity Loans


If you already own a home, a[home equity loan](https://www.pennymac.com/refinancing-products/home-equity-loans) lets you convert some of your equity into accessible funds. The money can be used for debt consolidation or to pay for significant expenses such as home renovations or tuition.


With a home equity loan, you can:


- Receive the funds as a one-time lump sum
- Rely on a fixed interest rate and predictable monthly principal and interest payments
- Keep your existing first mortgage and its interest rate unchanged


A home equity loan is essentially a second mortgage, so you’ll make a separate payment in addition to your existing mortgage.


Another way homeowners can access their equity is through a[cash-out refinance](https://www.pennymac.com/refinancing-products/cash-out-refinance) . It replaces your existing mortgage with a new, larger loan and gives you the difference in cash, minus any applicable costs. Cash-out refinancing is available with several loan types, including conventional, FHA, VA and jumbo loans.


## How Do You Choose the Right Home Loan?


The lowest interest rate isn’t the only factor to consider when comparing home loans. Your budget, down payment, credit, preferred loan structure, future plans and eligibility for specific programs can all help narrow your options. Look at the overall cost of each loan, including any mortgage insurance or other fees that may apply.


### How Much Can You Afford to Put Down?


Figure out what you can comfortably put toward a home while leaving room for closing costs, emergency savings and other expenses. You don’t necessarily need 20% down.


Down payment options vary by loan type:


- **[Conventional loans](https://www.pennymac.com/blog/what-is-a-conventional-loan) :** May allow down payments as low as 3% for qualified borrowers. Putting at least 20% down may help you avoid private mortgage insurance (PMI).
- **FHA loans:** May allow down payments as low as 3.5% for qualified borrowers.
- **VA loans:** Eligible borrowers may be able to buy a home with no down payment.


A larger down payment can reduce the amount you need to borrow and your monthly principal and interest payment. Also consider the other costs that may be part of your monthly housing expenses, including property taxes, homeowners insurance, mortgage insurance and HOA fees, if applicable.


Depending on where you live and your eligibility, a[down payment assistance program](https://www.pennymac.com/blog/affordable-lending-homebuyer-assistance-programs) may also help with upfront homebuying costs. Programs may offer grants, loans or other assistance and have their own income, purchase price and eligibility requirements.


### Do You Prefer a Fixed or Adjustable Interest Rate?


Think about how long you expect to keep the loan and how comfortable you are with the possibility that your rate will change.


- **Payment predictability:** A fixed-rate mortgage keeps the same interest rate for the life of the loan, so your monthly principal and interest payment stays consistent.
- **Initial rate:** An ARM starts with a fixed rate for a set period and may offer a lower initial rate than a comparable fixed-rate mortgage.
- **Future plans:** If you expect to move, sell or refinance before the fixed period ends, an ARM’s lower initial rate may be appealing. If refinancing is part of your plan, consider how long it may take to reach the break-even point, when the potential savings from refinancing offset the[closing costs](https://www.pennymac.com/blog/cost-to-refinance-mortgage) .


### Do You Qualify for a Government-Backed Loan?


FHA and VA loans are government-backed mortgages that can expand your home loan options if you meet their requirements. Eligibility, down payment requirements and loan costs differ between the two.


- **FHA loans:** Qualified borrowers may be able to put as little as 3.5% down and qualify with more flexible credit requirements. FHA loans require upfront and annual mortgage insurance premiums.
- **VA loans:** Eligible veterans, service members and certain surviving spouses may be able to buy with $0 down and no monthly mortgage insurance. A VA funding fee may apply, although some borrowers are exempt.


## FAQs About Home Loan Options


### Can First-Time Buyers Choose From Different Types of Home Loans?


Yes. First-time homebuyers can consider conventional, FHA, VA and other mortgage options based on their finances and eligibility. You don’t have to choose a particular loan type simply because you’re buying your first home.


### What Credit Score Do You Need for a Home Loan?


There’s no single credit score required for every home loan. Minimum credit scores vary by loan type and lender, and a higher score may help you qualify for more favorable rates and loan terms.


### Can You Change Your Loan Type During the Mortgage Process?


You may be able to change loan programs before closing if you qualify for the new loan. Talk with your loan officer as early as possible because changing programs may affect your documentation requirements, loan terms, costs or closing timeline.


## Compare Your Home Loan Options With Pennymac


Buying, refinancing or tapping into your home equity can call for different types of financing. Knowing what’s available can help you focus on the loan that fits what you want to do next.
